text: This is a great white shark. Cut perfectly in half. It's one of the most feared animals on Earth, but most people have never seen what's actually inside one. Everything you're about to see is inside every great white swimming right now. Let's open it, one part at a time.
First, the basics. Length: up to about six meters. Weight: up to about two tons. Teeth in its mouth right now: around three hundred. And bones… Zero.

A great white has no bones at all. Its whole skeleton is cartilage, the same bendy stuff in your nose and ears. Cartilage is lighter than bone and more flexible, so the shark can turn tight and fast. The spine is the one place where the cartilage gets hardened with minerals. And it grows in rings, like a tree. Scientists count those rings to estimate a shark's age. Some great whites live past seventy.

Now the skin. Run your hand from head to tail, it feels smooth. Tail to head, it feels like sandpaper. That's because the skin is covered in millions of tiny scales called denticles. And here's the strange part: each one is built like a tiny tooth. They channel the water in neat lines, which helps the shark slip through it with less drag.

Speaking of teeth. Behind the front row, there are more rows, folded back and waiting. When a front tooth breaks or falls out, the one behind it rolls forward to take its place. It's not a set of teeth. It's a conveyor belt.
Sharks lose teeth all the time, and they never run out. Over a lifetime, a great white can go through thousands of them. Which is why shark teeth are some of the most common fossils on Earth.

So how hard can it bite? No one can safely put a meter in a great white's mouth, so scientists built a computer model of its jaw. Their estimate for a large shark: about eighteen thousand newtons. A strong human bite is around one thousand.

Now look at the biggest thing inside the body. It's not the stomach. It's not the heart. It's the liver. It can make up about a quarter of the shark's entire weight. Most fish float with a gas-filled swim bladder. Sharks don't have one. Instead, the liver is packed with oil, and oil is lighter than seawater. It works like a built-in float. And it doubles as a fuel tank. On long ocean crossings, great whites burn that oil for energy.

Now look at the fins. The two big fins behind the head are not paddles. They work like the wings of a plane. As the shark moves forward, water flows over them and creates lift, so the heavy front end doesn't sink. The tall fin on its back works like a keel. It stops the body from rolling. And the tail is shaped like a crescent moon, almost the same on top and bottom. That shape is built for one thing. Speed.

With that tail, a great white can sprint at around forty kilometers per hour in short bursts. Off the coast of South Africa, they hunt seals by rushing up from the deep so fast that they launch their whole body out of the water. Two tons, completely airborne.

Behind the head, five gill slits on each side. Water goes in through the mouth, over the gills, and out the slits. The gills pull the oxygen out of it. But a great white can't pump water over its gills the way many fish can. It has to keep swimming, with its mouth slightly open, to push the water through. Stop swimming, and the water stops.

That oxygen is pushed around the body by a small heart with two main chambers. Your heart sends blood around two loops. A shark's heart sends it around just one: heart, gills, body, and back to the heart.

And now something most fish can't do. Fish are usually the same temperature as the water around them. A great white isn't. Around its swimming muscles, a dense net of blood vessels works like a heat exchanger. Warm blood leaving the muscles heats the cold blood coming in, so the heat stays inside. Parts of its body can stay up to about fourteen degrees warmer than the ocean. Warm muscles are faster muscles. That's how it can explode upward from below.

Food goes down into a U-shaped stomach. Some sharks can even push their stomach out through their mouth to rinse it, then pull it back in. After the stomach comes the strangest organ of all: the spiral valve. Instead of a long, coiled tube like ours, the gut is short and twisted inside like a corkscrew. Food has to spin its way through, which gives the shark more time to absorb everything.
Its menu changes as it grows. Young great whites mostly eat fish. But once they pass about three meters, their teeth change shape, from narrow and pointed to broad and serrated. Perfect for seals.

That oil-filled liver also lets great whites travel incredibly far. In two thousand three, scientists tagged a female named Nicole off South Africa. She swam all the way to Australia, and came back. About twenty thousand kilometers, in under nine months.

Now the senses. Look at the snout. Those dark dots are pores. Each one leads to a jelly-filled canal called an ampulla of Lorenzini. They sense electricity. Every living animal's muscles give off a tiny electric field. Even a fish hiding under the sand. These pores can pick up fields of just a few billionths of a volt.

Along both sides of the body runs a line of sensors called the lateral line. It feels pressure waves in the water. A struggling fish far away sends ripples that the shark can feel before it ever sees it.

Inside the head, the brain is small. But look at the front of it. These two bulbs are just for smell. In great whites, they make up a big share of the whole brain. It doesn't just smell the ocean. It reads it.

Behind each eye sits a mirror-like layer that bounces light back through the eye, so it can see in dim water. And when it bites, a great white rolls its eyes back into its head to protect them. For that split second, it bites blind.
Great whites don't only look underwater. Sometimes a shark lifts its head straight out of the water and looks around at the surface. Scientists call it spy-hopping.

Put all of these senses together, and you get a hunting sequence. Smell works from far away. Then the lateral line feels the movement. Then the eyes lock on. And in the last few centimeters, when the eyes roll back, electricity guides the bite.

And one last part, found only in females. Great white babies grow inside their mother. Before they're born, the pups feed on unfertilized eggs that she keeps producing. Pregnancy may last more than a year. When they're finally born, they're already over a meter long, with a full set of teeth. And they swim away on their own. No parents. No lessons.

Sharks, as a group, have been around for more than four hundred million years. That's older than trees. And great whites take their time. Females may not have their first pups until they're over thirty. This design has been tested longer than almost anything alive.
No bones. Teeth on its skin. A liver that floats. Muscles that run warm. A sixth sense for electricity. This is what's inside a great white shark. Next specimen? Tell us what we should open.
